summary: This standards-track memo defines the vemmi URL scheme for VEMMI, an international standard for online multimedia services. It lets a link point to such a service the way an http link points to a web page.

eli5.summary: A new kind of web address that opens one special type of online service.

questions: what is the vemmi url scheme
subtitle: A URL scheme that lets a link start a VEMMI multimedia session, and the login dialog that follows.

tldr.problem: VEMMI multimedia services had no standard way to be named in a link, so Web browsers and VEMMI terminals could not be pointed at them.
tldr.mechanism: The vemmi URL scheme names a host, an optional port (default 575), an optional service and optional attribute=value parameters. The client then answers simple text prompts from the host.
tldr.outcome: A Web page can hold a vemmi link that starts a VEMMI client. The RFC also describes the application/vemmi media type for exchanging VEMMI objects.

today: RFC 2122 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata for this RFC lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the URL rules in RFC 1738.

sections.title: What VEMMI Is
sections.content:
RFC 2122 defines a new URL scheme, vemmi. It lets VEMMI client software and terminals connect to services that follow the VEMMI standard, which stands for Enhanced Man-Machine Interface for Videotex and Multimedia/Hypermedia Information Retrieval Services and is sometimes abbreviated as VErsatile MultiMedia Interface.

The RFC describes VEMMI as an international standard (ITU-T T.107 and the European standard ETS 300 382, obsoleted by ETS 300 709) for on-line multimedia services. It covers both the man-machine interface and the client/server exchange protocol, usually over a single continuous session, and is object-oriented, event-driven and platform independent. IANA has assigned TCP port 575 to it.
sections.eli5: VEMMI is a way for a computer to show a rich, picture-filled online service. This RFC just gives such services an address you can click.

sections.title: Why a URL Scheme
sections.content:
The RFC lists three uses. First, service selection: one server can host several VEMMI applications, so after connecting the terminal needs to pick one, and the URL is the best way to describe that service. Second, reporting user actions: VEMMI normally reports actions over its own link, but a client that browses HTML documents inside a VEMMI dialog box may need a URL to report actions to the server or to another system.

Third, extending Web browsers: VEMMI is described as complementary to HTTP and HTML, and with a vemmi URL a browser can start a VEMMI client module when the user activates a link in an HTML document.
sections.eli5: A server can run many different services, so you need a way to say which one you want. A web page also needs a way to hand you over to it.

sections.title: The vemmi URL Syntax
sections.content:
A VEMMI URL takes the form vemmi://<host>:<port>/<vemmiservice>;<attribute>=<value>, following Section 3.1 of RFC 1738. If the port is omitted it defaults to 575, though client software may ignore the port to increase security. The service part is optional.

The URL does not name a data object. It names a multimedia interactive service, and the link between client and server is usually kept for the whole session. If the service name is omitted and the server asks for it, the client is expected to prompt the user.

Parameters follow the service, each starting with a semicolon, with the attribute and value joined by =. Attribute names are case-insensitive; values may or may not be, depending on the attribute. Names beginning with $ are reserved: $COMMAND, $CONTEXTDATA, $OBJECT_REQUEST and $USERDATA. A username and password cannot be put in the URL for security reasons.
sections.eli5: The address names the computer, then optionally the service you want, then optional extra notes. It never contains your password.

sections.title: The Service Selection Dialog
sections.content:
After connecting, the client is in standard mode and may show text from the network in a videotex or telnet terminal window. Service selection is a simple prompt-and-answer dialog, so it works over a telnet or videotex compatible session. The host may send the prompt strings service:, username: and password:. The client answers each, automatically if the answer is known or by asking the user. Any URL parameters are sent after the service name in the answer to service:, separated by a semicolon.

  • Every answer must end with a Carriage Return. A Line Feed after the CR is ignored by the server.
  • The server may echo the characters, with the CR echoed as CR LF, and may echo passwords as stars or other scrambled output.
  • The client must be ready to start the VEMMI session as soon as it receives the VEMMI_Open command.

If activation fails, the host may display the cause. The RFC recommends the HTTP status code syntax (RFC 1945, RFC 2068) where possible so clients can process the answer automatically. Using HTTP to carry VEMMI objects or session data is mentioned as possible, but is not described.
sections.eli5: The server asks questions one at a time, like which service and what your name is. The client answers each one and ends each answer with a Return key press.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives four informational examples. For vemmi://zeus.mctel.fr/demo, the host asks service:, the client answers demo, and the host returns 200 OK. For vemmi://zeus.mctel.fr with no service, the host starts the session at once, and the client would prompt the user only if the host asked for a service.

A URL such as vemmi://mctel.fr/demo carries no credentials, so if the host asks, the client may use a default or prompt the user, for instance proposing anonymous and the user's e-mail address. In the RFC's example the host answers 401 Unauthorized. A URL with parameters, vemmi://mctel.fr/demo;$USERDATA=smith;account=1234, makes the client answer service: with demo;$USERDATA=smith;account=1234.
sections.eli5: If the address names a service, the client just says its name when asked. If there is no password in the address, the client asks you for one.

sections.title: Browsers Without VEMMI Support and the Media Type
sections.content:
A browser that does not know the scheme may signal an error, or may treat the link as a relative URL and ask the originating host for it, which usually gives a not found error. The RFC suggests that a server can be modified to offer a VEMMI client download in that case, that an HTML page can offer both a vemmi link and a download link, or that a server can check whether the HTTP Accept header includes application/vemmi.

The RFC also defines the application/vemmi media type, with no required parameters and an optional version=<integer> such as version=100. VEMMI uses a native 8-bit binary format, so base64 is preferred, although 7-bit transmission is possible. For browsers that cannot add new URL schemes, the type can carry a text file containing the vemmi URL. At the time of writing, registration with IANA was pending.
sections.eli5: Older browsers may not understand the new kind of address. The RFC suggests friendly ways to hand them a download or a file that points the way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The vemmi scheme has the same security implications as URLs in general, so the usual precautions apply, such as not storing a username and password in a URL. VEMMI sessions can also download metacode objects (sequences of VEMMI commands) and operative objects, which are executable programs run on the client. The RFC strongly recommends that users disable running operative objects from potentially unsafe sources, or at least require approval first.

Username and password identification is described as unsecure and provided for backwards compatibility only. Services that need safe identification must rely on other mechanisms such as S/KEY.
sections.eli5: Some things a service sends are actual programs. Be careful to only run them if you trust where they came from, and do not put passwords in addresses.

data.title: vemmi URL syntax
data.code:
vemmiurl      = "vemmi://" hostport [ "/" vemmiservice *[ parameter ] ]
vemmiservice  = *[ uchar | "/" | "?" | ":" | "@" | "&" | "=" ]
parameter     = ";" attribute "=" value
attribute     = *[ uchar | "/" | "?" | ":" | "@" | "&" ]
value         = *[ uchar | "/" | "?" | ":" | "@" | "&" ]
